# Data Visualization with ggplot2

### Graphical Perception & Publication-Ready Figures

**Chapter 4 · From Data to Thesis**

Dr. Polla Fattah

---

## Why Numerical Summaries Are Not Enough

A table of 600 numbers says almost nothing at a glance.

A well-crafted figure reveals within seconds:

- Where most values cluster.
- The degree of spread and dispersion.
- Outliers, data entry errors, and multimodal distributions.
- Non-linear relationships that Pearson correlations conceal.

> **Graphs are not cosmetic decorations added at the end of a project; they are primary instruments of scientific reasoning.**

---

## Anscombe's Quartet (1973)

Francis Anscombe constructed four synthetic datasets to demonstrate that identical summary statistics can describe radically different realities:

| Metric | Dataset 1 | Dataset 2 | Dataset 3 | Dataset 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mean of X** | 9.00 | 9.00 | 9.00 | 9.00 |
| **Mean of Y** | 7.50 | 7.50 | 7.50 | 7.50 |
| **Variance of X** | 11.00 | 11.00 | 11.00 | 11.00 |
| **Variance of Y** | 4.13 | 4.13 | 4.13 | 4.13 |
| **Correlation ($r$)** | **0.82** | **0.82** | **0.82** | **0.82** |
| **Regression line** | $y = 3 + 0.5x$ | $y = 3 + 0.5x$ | $y = 3 + 0.5x$ | $y = 3 + 0.5x$ |

*Judged purely by the numbers, all four datasets appear identical!*

---

## Seeing Anscombe's Quartet in R

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

anscombe_long <- tibble(
  set = rep(paste("Set", 1:4), each = 11),
  x   = c(anscombe$x1, anscombe$x2, anscombe$x3, anscombe$x4),
  y   = c(anscombe$y1, anscombe$y2, anscombe$y3, anscombe$y4)
)

ggplot(anscombe_long, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ set) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

```
+-------------------+-------------------+
| Set 1: Standard   | Set 2: Curvilinear|
| linear scatter    | quadratic parabola|
+-------------------+-------------------+
| Set 3: Strict line| Set 4: Vertical   |
| + 1 extreme outlier| column + 1 anchor |
+-------------------+-------------------+
```

Only Set 1 satisfies the assumptions of linear correlation. **Looking first is not optional.**

---

## Exploratory vs. Explanatory Graphics

Scientific visualization serves two distinct purposes:

### 1. Exploratory Graphics (For the Researcher)
- Produced rapidly in large volumes during data analysis.
- Goal: diagnose missingness, test distribution shapes, detect coding bugs.
- Minimal polish required; speed and iteration are key.

### 2. Explanatory Graphics (For the Reader & Thesis Committee)
- Selected carefully from dozens of exploratory iterations.
- Goal: communicate one core substantive insight with maximum clarity.
- Demands rigorous labeling, accessible palettes, and disciplined layout.

---

# Graphical Perception

### The Cognitive Science of How Humans Read Data

---

## The Cleveland & McGill Hierarchy (1984)

William Cleveland and Robert McGill conducted psychophysical experiments to measure how accurately the human eye decodes quantitative information:

```
MOST ACCURATE
   ^    1. Position along a common scale  (Scatter plots, dot plots)
   |    2. Position along non-aligned scales (Facets, small multiples)
   |    3. Length                         (Bar charts)
   |    4. Direction / Angle / Slope      (Line charts, pie slices)
   |    5. Area                           (Bubble charts)
   v    6. Volume / 3D Perspective        (3D bar charts - AVOID)
LEAST   7. Color saturation & shading     (Heat maps)
ACCURATE
```

> **Core Rule:** Always encode your primary research comparison into **position along a common scale** or **length**.

---

## The Pie Chart vs. Bar Chart Experiment

Why do statisticians and journal editors advise against pie charts?

- In a **pie chart**, the brain must evaluate angles and surface areas.
- When slices are close (e.g., 23%, 21%, 20%, 19%, 17%), ranking them requires reading the legend or numerical labels.
- In a **bar chart**, the exact same numbers are encoded as lengths along a shared baseline:

```
Pie Chart:                  Bar Chart (Shared Baseline):
     ( )                        A |======================= (23%)
  ( 21% | 23% )                 B |=====================   (21%)
 (------+------)                C |====================    (20%)
  ( 19% | 20% )                 D |===================     (19%)
     ( 17% )                    E |=================       (17%)
(Hard to order!)            (Immediate, effortless perceptual ranking!)
```

---

## Principles of Honest Data Encoding

### 1. Align Comparisons on a Single Baseline
Comparing bars across separate pages or separate unaligned panels introduces cognitive error.

### 2. Avoid Area-Based Encodings
Doubling the diameter of a circle quadruples its area ($A = \pi r^2$), exaggerating differences by a factor of 4.

### 3. Color as Categorical Distinction, Not Magnitude
Use color to distinguish 2–5 discrete groups. Do not rely on subtle color shades to convey precise quantitative values.

---

# Choosing the Right Graph

### Matching Research Questions to Geometries

---

## Decision Matrix for Scientific Plots

| Research Question | Variable Types | Recommended Graph | ggplot2 Geom |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distribution of 1 metric | 1 Numeric | Histogram, Density plot | `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` |
| Counts across categories | 1 Categorical | Bar chart | `geom_bar()`, `geom_col()` |
| Group differences | Numeric by Categorical | Box plot, Jittered strip plot | `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_jitter()` |
| Bivariate association | 2 Numeric | Scatter plot + Trend line | `geom_point()`, `geom_smooth()` |
| Longitudinal trajectory | Numeric over Time | Line chart | `geom_line()`, `geom_point()` |
| High-dimensional matrix | Many Numeric | Correlation heat map | `geom_tile()`, `geom_text()` |

---

# The Grammar of Graphics

### The Conceptual Foundation of ggplot2

---

## What is the "Grammar of Graphics"?

Created by Leland Wilkinson (2005) and implemented in R by Hadley Wickham:

> **A statistical graphic is a mapping from data variables to visual aesthetic properties of geometric objects.**

Every plot in ggplot2 is built from three core components:

1. **Data:** A tidy data frame or tibble.
2. **Aesthetic Mappings (`aes()`):** Which variable links to `x`, `y`, `colour`, `fill`, `shape`, `size`.
3. **Geometric Layers (`geoms`):** Visual marks representing data (`point`, `bar`, `line`, `boxplot`).

---

## Building a Plot Step-by-Step

Consider a pilot study of 5 students:

```r
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

pilot <- tibble(
  student = c("S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"),
  sleep   = c(6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0),
  stress  = c(3.2, 2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 3.9)
)
```

Step 1: Define data and aesthetic mappings:

```r
# Generates an empty canvas with calibrated axes, but NO data marks:
ggplot(data = pilot, mapping = aes(x = sleep, y = stress))
```

---

## Adding the Geometric Layer

Step 2: Add geometric marks with the `+` operator:

```r
ggplot(pilot, aes(x = sleep, y = stress)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, colour = "navy")
```

```
Stress
 4.5 |       * (S3: 5.5h, 4.5)
     |
 3.5 |           * (S5: 6.0h, 3.9)
     |             * (S1: 6.5h, 3.2)
 2.5 |                 * (S2: 7.5h, 2.1)
     |                     * (S4: 8.0h, 1.8)
 1.5 +--------------------------------------
     5.0    6.0    7.0    8.0   Sleep (hrs)
```

Adding layers with `+` allows modular composition: points, trend lines, error bars, and labels stack seamlessly.

---

# Core Geometries for Empirical Research

### Histograms, Bars, Boxes, Scatters, and Lines

---

## Histograms: Inspecting Distributions

Histograms partition continuous variables into contiguous **bins** and count observations in each bin:

```r
library(data2thesis)

first_sem <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 1) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id))

ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sleep per night (hours)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

### The Sensitivity of `binwidth`
- **Too wide (`binwidth = 3`):** Masks skewness and multimodality.
- **Too narrow (`binwidth = 0.05`):** Introduces distracting random sampling noise.
- **Best Practice:** Test 3 to 4 binwidths before choosing the explanatory view.

---

## Bar Charts: `geom_bar()` vs. `geom_col()`

Understanding the distinction between counting and displaying pre-calculated values:

### 1. `geom_bar()`: R Computes Frequencies Automatically
```r
# Given raw categorical rows, geom_bar() tabulates counts:
ggplot(students, aes(x = faculty)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40")
```

### 2. `geom_col()`: You Supply Pre-Calculated Heights
```r
faculty_summary <- students |> count(faculty)

ggplot(faculty_summary, aes(x = faculty, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue")
```

Both produce identical plots, but `geom_col()` is used when displaying means or percentages.

---

## Box Plots: Visualizing Group Differences

The Tukey box plot summarizes five key statistics:

```
       Outlier (*) > 1.5 * IQR above Q3
          |
     +----+----+   Upper Whisker (highest non-outlier)
     |         |   Third Quartile (Q3, 75th percentile)
     |=========|   MEDIAN (Q2, 50th percentile)
     |         |   First Quartile (Q1, 25th percentile)
     +----+----+   Lower Whisker (lowest non-outlier)
          |
       Outlier (*) < 1.5 * IQR below Q1
```

```r
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = study_mode, y = wellbeing)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", colour = "grey30", width = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Study Mode", y = "Wellbeing (0–100)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

---

## Scatter Plots & Overplotting

When plotting 600 students, points clump and overlap (**overplotting**):

```r
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours, y = gpa)) +
  # alpha = 0.4 adds transparency: dense regions become darker
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 2, colour = "navy") +
  # method = "lm" draws an ordinary least squares linear regression line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "darkred", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Sleep (hours)", y = "Grade Point Average (GPA)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- `alpha` ranges from 0 (invisible) to 1 (opaque).
- `se = TRUE` renders the 95% confidence interval ribbon around the trend line.

---

## Longitudinal Trajectories with Line Charts

Visualizing cohort changes across time:

```r
wellbeing_by_sem <- semesters |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |>
  summarise(mean_wellbeing = mean(wellbeing), .by = c(semester, workshop))

ggplot(wellbeing_by_sem, aes(x = semester, y = mean_wellbeing, colour = workshop)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Semester", y = "Mean Wellbeing", colour = "Workshop Cohort") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- Connecting points with lines implies continuous time or sequential progression.
- Never use line charts across unordered categorical groups (e.g., across faculties)!

---

# The Classic Pitfall: Mapping vs. Setting

### Why Does My Plot Turn Salmon Pink?

---

## Aesthetic Mapping vs. Fixed Aesthetic Setting

### The Error: Putting Fixed Values Inside `aes()`
```r
# WRONG:
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours, fill = "steelblue")) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)
```

**What happens?**

1. ggplot2 interprets `"steelblue"` not as a color, but as a categorical variable containing one level.
2. It assigns that level the default categorical color (salmon pink).
3. It adds a nonsensical legend labeled `"fill: steelblue"`.

---

## The Correct Rule

```
INSIDE aes()   ==> Dynamic: Value depends on data variable
                   Example: aes(colour = workshop, size = gpa)

OUTSIDE aes()  ==> Fixed: Value is constant across all marks
                   Example: geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3)
```

```r
# RIGHT:
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white")
```

All bars are rendered in steelblue, with white borders, and no redundant legend.

---

# Polishing Explanatory Graphs for Publication

### Labels, Scales, Themes, and Annotations

---

## The Four Pillars of Publication Polish

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. LABELS      | Meaningful titles, units on axes (labs)    |
| 2. SCALES      | Discontinuous breaks, colorblind palettes  |
| 3. THEMES      | Clean backgrounds, legible font sizes      |
| 4. ANNOTATIONS | Explicit thresholds & reference lines      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Pillar 1: Comprehensive Labeling with `labs()`

Never leave raw code variable names (`sleep_hours`, `gpa`, `n`) on a thesis figure:

```r
p <- ggplot(wellbeing_by_sem, aes(x = semester, y = mean_wellbeing, colour = workshop)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "Student Wellbeing Trajectory Over Two Years",
    subtitle = "Mean wellbeing score (0–100) per semester, stratified by workshop intervention",
    x        = "Academic Semester",
    y        = "Average Wellbeing Score",
    colour   = "Intervention Group",
    caption  = "Source: Graduate Wellbeing Longitudinal Study (N = 600)"
  )
```

---

## Pillar 2: Scales & Colorblind Accessibility

Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Standard green/red palettes fail accessibility tests.

```r
p <- p +
  # Force integer ticks on the semester axis:
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4) +
  # Apply perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe Viridis palette:
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.8)
```

Viridis palettes:

- Remain distinct under deuteranopia, protanopia, and tritanopia.
- Convert cleanly to greyscale when printed on monochrome laser printers.

---

## Pillar 3: Academic Theme Styling

The default grey grid of ggplot2 is intended for interactive screen exploration, not formal dissertations:

```r
p <- p +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position    = "bottom",
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    axis.title         = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

- `base_size = 13`: Scales all text elements proportionally.
- `legend.position = "bottom"`: Widens the plot plotting area.

---

## Pillar 4: Direct Graphical Annotations

Guide the reader's eye directly to substantive thresholds:

```r
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  # Reference line at recommended sleep:
  geom_vline(xintercept = 7.0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  # Direct text annotation:
  annotate(
    "text", x = 7.15, y = Inf, 
    label = "Recommended Minimum: 7.0 hrs", 
    hjust = 0, vjust = 1.8, colour = "firebrick", fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Sleep (hours/night)", y = "Number of Students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

`y = Inf` automatically pins the text to the top edge of the plot coordinate space regardless of histogram height.

---

# Honest vs. Misleading Visualizations

### Case Study: Detecting and Correcting Visual Distortion

---

## The Four Cardinal Sins of Visual Distortion

### 1. Truncated Baselines on Bar Charts
A bar encodes value through its length. Truncating the y-axis (e.g., starting at 58 instead of 0) turns a 3% difference into an apparent 300% surge.

### 2. Distorted Aspect Ratios
Stretching or compressing axes exaggerates or flattens regression slopes.

### 3. Chartjunk & 3D Extrusion
Drop shadows, 3D perspective tilts, and decorative clip art distort angles and obscure measurement points.

### 4. Rainbow Palettes (Jet / Rainbow)
Rainbow colormaps introduce sharp artificial boundaries that do not correspond to true discontinuities in the underlying data.

---

## The "Before" Attempt: The Truncated Bar Chart

```r
faculty_means <- first_sem |>
  summarise(wellbeing = mean(wellbeing), .by = faculty)

# MISLEADING: Truncated axis from 58 to 62.5
ggplot(faculty_means, aes(x = faculty, y = wellbeing, fill = faculty)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(58, 62.5))
```

```
Wellbeing
62.5 |      [====]              [====]
60.0 |      [====]    [====]    [====]
58.0 +----------------------------------
          Education  Health   Humanities
     (Education looks 4x taller than Health!)
```

**The Reality:** The means differ by only 1.8 points on a 100-point instrument.

---

## The "After" Redesign: The Honest Strip Plot

```r
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = wellbeing, y = reorder(faculty, wellbeing))) +
  # 1. Show individual student variation with faint jittered points:
  geom_jitter(height = 0.18, alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  # 2. Overlay group means prominently in red:
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3.5, colour = "firebrick") +
  # 3. Informative labels and clean styling:
  labs(
    title    = "Student Wellbeing Across Academic Faculties",
    subtitle = "Individual student scores (grey points) with faculty group means (red dots)",
    x        = "Wellbeing Score (Semester 1, 0–100 Scale)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

**Substantive Truth Revealed:** The variance *within* faculties is vast (scores from 25 to 95); the variance *between* faculty means is negligible.

---

# Advanced Visualization Techniques

### Small Multiples, Density Curves, and Correlation Tiles

---

## Small Multiples with `facet_wrap()`

Faceting partitions a dataset into separate panels sharing identical scale axes:

```r
ggplot(first_sem, aes(x = sleep_hours, y = gpa)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = "navy") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "firebrick", se = FALSE) +
  # Split across degree programme:
  facet_wrap(~ programme) +
  labs(x = "Sleep Hours", y = "Cumulative GPA") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- Facilitates parallel visual comparisons without overlapping clutter.
- For 2 grouping variables (e.g., `programme` $\times$ `study_mode`), use `facet_grid(programme ~ study_mode)`.

---

## Density Plots: Comparing Distributions

`geom_density()` calculates a smoothed kernel density estimate:

```r
semesters |>
  filter(semester == 2) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = wellbeing, fill = workshop)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Wellbeing Distribution Following Workshop (Semester 2)",
    x     = "Wellbeing Score", 
    y     = "Probability Density", 
    fill  = "Workshop Cohort"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Reveals that the entire intervention distribution shifted rightward, not just a subset of high performers.

---

## Correlation Heat Maps with `geom_tile()`

Visualizing multi-variable association matrices:

```r
library(tidyr)

cor_matrix <- first_sem |>
  select(gpa, sleep_hours, study_hours, wellbeing) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

cor_long <- cor_matrix |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(var1 = rownames(cor_matrix)) |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 4.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Pearson r") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The diverging color gradient (`scale_fill_gradient2`) highlights positive associations in red, negative in blue, and zero correlation in neutral white.

# Exporting High-Resolution Figures

### Preparing Graphics for Dissertations and Journals

---

## `ggsave()`: Syntax and Parameters

Never take low-resolution screenshots of RStudio graphics! Use `ggsave()`:

```r
# Vector PDF for lossless print quality:
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/fig01_wellbeing_trajectory.pdf",
  plot     = p,
  width    = 16,
  height   = 10,
  units    = "cm"
)

# High-resolution raster PNG for web or Word submissions (300 DPI):
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/fig01_wellbeing_trajectory.png",
  plot     = p,
  width    = 16,
  height   = 10,
  units    = "cm",
  dpi      = 300
)
```

---

## Vector vs. Raster Formats

| Format | Extension | Type | Scalability | Best Used For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PDF** | `.pdf` | Vector | Infinite (lossless zoom) | LaTeX, Quarto, Journal Print |
| **SVG** | `.svg` | Vector | Infinite (web native) | HTML presentations, Websites |
| **PNG** | `.png` | Raster | Fixed (300+ DPI recommended) | Word documents, PowerPoints |
| **TIFF** | `.tiff` | Raster | Uncompressed | Medical/Biology Journals |

### Sizing Guidelines:
- Single-column journal figure: ~8–9 cm width.
- Two-column / Full-page thesis figure: ~15–17 cm width.

# Real-World Extension: Macroeconomics

### Visualizing Temporal Shocks with `economics`

---

## The `economics` Dataset

ggplot2 includes historical US macroeconomic records (1967–2015):

```r
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(colour = "navy", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title    = "United States Unemployment Over Time",
    subtitle = "Number of unemployed civilians in thousands (1967–2015)",
    x        = "Year",
    y        = "Unemployed (Thousands)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

**Substantive Nuance:** The plot displays absolute raw counts, not the unemployment *rate*. Because population doubled between 1967 and 2015, the 2008 peak looks disproportionately massive. Clear axis labels prevent analytical misinterpretation.

---

# Thesis Figure Checklist & Chapter Review

---

## The Thesis Figure Defense Checklist

Before binding figures into your thesis document:

- [ ] **Accurate Baseline:** Bar charts start strictly at zero.
- [ ] **No Raw Column Names:** Every axis displays plain English and metric units.
- [ ] **Accessible Color Palette:** Viridis or colorblind-verified custom scales.
- [ ] **Visible Data Variance:** Averages are accompanied by standard error bars or jittered points.
- [ ] **Resolved Overplotting:** Transparency (`alpha`) applied to dense scatter plots.
- [ ] **Appropriate Geometry:** Lines reserved for temporal/sequential data; bars for counts; boxes for distributions.
- [ ] **High Resolution:** Vector PDF or 300+ DPI raster export.

---

## Summary of Core ggplot2 Functions

| Purpose | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Initialize canvas | `ggplot()` | `ggplot(data, aes(x, y))` |
| Draw points | `geom_point()` | `geom_point(alpha = 0.4)` |
| Draw bars / columns | `geom_bar()`, `geom_col()` | `geom_col(fill = "steelblue")` |
| Draw boxplots | `geom_boxplot()` | `geom_boxplot(width = 0.5)` |
| Draw lines | `geom_line()` | `geom_line(linewidth = 1)` |
| Draw smooth trend | `geom_smooth()` | `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` |
| Partition panels | `facet_wrap()` | `facet_wrap(~ programme)` |
| Set labels | `labs()` | `labs(title = "...", x = "...")` |
| Colorblind scale | `scale_colour_viridis_d()` | `scale_colour_viridis_d()` |
| Clean theme | `theme_minimal()` | `theme_minimal(base_size = 13)` |
| Save figure | `ggsave()` | `ggsave("fig.pdf", width=16, height=10, units="cm")` |
